Tree plot

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/tree-plot.Rmd
tree-plot.Rmd

Class enumeration estimates one mixture model for each number of classes. Each model is fitted from its own starting values, and the numbering of its classes is arbitrary, so class 2 of a three-class solution has no defined relation to class 2 of a four-class solution. The relation between two solutions is carried by the observations they classify. When the classes of the larger solution subdivide those of the smaller one, each class of the smaller solution passes its members to one or more classes of the larger, and the solutions are nested. When the larger solution redistributes observations across class boundaries, the classes of the two solutions overlap without nesting. A clustering tree represents these relations for a sequence of solutions (Zappia and Oshlack, 2018). Each row of the tree is one solution, divided into its classes in proportion to their size, and the band between two classes in adjacent rows is proportional to the observations they share.

In a mixture model each observation belongs to every class with a posterior probability. For two solutions AA and BB fitted to the same NN observations, with posterior probabilities piap_{ia} and qibq_{ib} and observation weights wiw_i, the shared posterior mass of class aa of AA and class bb of BB is

mab=∑i=1Nwipiaqib∑i=1Nwi.m_{ab} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \, p_{ia} \, q_{ib}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i}.

The masses form a joint distribution over the pairs of classes. Summed over the classes of BB, they give the posterior share of class aa, and summed over the classes of AA, the posterior share of class bb. The ratio of mabm_{ab} to the share of aa is the part of class aa that the larger solution places in class bb. A tree built from posterior probabilities retains the uncertainty of the classification, which a tree built from modal assignments discards.

A two-level mixture model has two sequences of solutions (Vermunt, 2003). Observations are classified into classes, and the groups that contain them are classified into group classes by their distribution over those classes. The classes form a tree at each number of group classes, and the group classes form a tree at each number of classes. Solutions can also be compared at a single level, for example the four-class solutions estimated with different numbers of group classes, whose classes need not coincide.

Data and candidates

student_esm holds experience-sampling data from 100 university students (Neubauer and Schmiedek, 2024). At each prompt when they had not studied since the previous one, the students reported which of eight leisure activities they had done. The prompts are the observations and the students the groups. The candidates combine one to six classes of prompts with one to four group classes of students.

library(latents)
activities <- c("time_with_friends", "on_social_media", "tv_video_games",
                "listened_music", "sports", "walking", "reading",
                "part_time_job")
models <- enumerate_classes(student_esm, activities, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:6, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            categorical = activities, n_starts = 3, seed = 1)

The grid holds 24 candidates. Their classes of prompts are counted by n_profiles, the name the package uses at both levels of a two-level model. The 3 candidates with one class and several group classes could not be estimated. A group class is defined by its distribution over the classes, and with a single class every group has the same distribution. Every tree with two or more group classes therefore begins at two classes.

The tree at one number of group classes

At one group class the model is a single-level latent class model of the prompts. Its tree shows how the classes of prompts divide as classes are added.

plot_tree(models, n_group_classes = 1)

plot_responses(get_candidate(models, n_profiles = 3, n_group_classes = 1),
               intervals = FALSE)

The two-class solution separates prompts with media use (social media, television or games, music) from prompts with offline activities. In the three-class solution the media class keeps 76% of its posterior mass. The offline class divides into three parts. The largest, 64%, forms a class of time with friends and walking, 27% joins the media class, and the remainder forms a class of 4% of prompts in which the probability of a part-time job is 1.00. The part-time job class passes 96% of its mass to a single class of the four-class solution, so it persists as further classes are added.

Every tree

Without a choice of group classes, each number of group classes has its own tree, returned as a separate plot. On an interactive screen device the plots are shown one at a time.

plot_tree(models)

A later tree matches its classes to those of the first tree using a one-to-one assignment of posterior overlap at the same number of classes. The assignment maximizes total overlap for square matches up to eight classes; larger or rectangular matches use a greedy assignment. A class can therefore be matched to something other than its own largest-overlap class. Colours mark these assigned correspondences. combine = TRUE plots every tree as a panel of one figure.

Comparing solutions at one level

A single value of n_profiles selects one level of every tree. The rows of the plot are then the solutions with that number of classes, one for each number of group classes, and the bands show where the same prompts are classified in each.

plot_tree(models, n_profiles = 4, n_group_classes = c(1, 3))

The values behind the plot are returned by get_results() with the same arguments, one row per pair of classes.

get_results(models, "tree", n_profiles = 4, n_group_classes = c(1, 3))

Each class of the four-class solution with one group class places between 45% and 88% of its posterior mass in a single class of the solution with three group classes. The two solutions describe similar classes, and the group classes shift a part of the prompts between them. Omitting n_group_classes compares the same level across every number of group classes.

plot_tree(models, n_profiles = 4)

Comparing two solutions

Any two candidates are compared with from and to, each given by its number of classes and number of group classes.

plot_tree(models, from = c(3, 1), to = c(4, 3))

The candidates can also be given by name, in the order of the rows, with candidates = c("classes3_groups1", "classes4_groups3").

The tree of group classes

With level = "groups" the units are the students and the classes are the group classes. A tree then runs down the numbers of group classes at one number of classes of prompts.

plot_tree(models, level = "groups", n_profiles = 4)

From two to three group classes, one group class of the three-group-class solution receives 98% of its students from a single group class of the two-group-class solution. The other group classes draw their students from both. The tree of group classes is read in the same way as the tree of classes. With level = "groups", a single value of n_group_classes compares one level of group classes across numbers of classes, as n_profiles does for the classes.

Summary of calls

Question Call
How do the classes divide as classes are added? plot_tree(models, n_group_classes = 1)
The same for every number of group classes plot_tree(models), combine = TRUE for one figure
How do the solutions with four classes differ across group classes? plot_tree(models, n_profiles = 4, n_group_classes = c(1, 3))
How do two chosen solutions correspond? plot_tree(models, from = c(3, 1), to = c(4, 3))
How do the group classes divide? plot_tree(models, level = "groups", n_profiles = 4)
The shared masses behind any of these get_results(models, "tree", ...) with the same arguments

Neubauer, A. B., & Schmiedek, F. (2024). Approaching academic adjustment on multiple time scales. Zeitschrift für Erziehungswissenschaft, 27(1), 147-168. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11618-023-01182-8

Vermunt, J. K. (2003). Multilevel latent class models. Sociological Methodology, 33, 213–239.

Zappia, L., & Oshlack, A. (2018). Clustering trees: A visualization for evaluating clusterings at multiple resolutions. GigaScience, 7(7), giy083.
